abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently shown strong potential in enabling robots to follow language instructions and execute precise actions. However, most VLAs are built upon vision-language models pretrained solely on 2D data, which lack accurate spatial awareness and hinder their ability to operate in the 3D physical world. Existing solutions attempt to incorporate explicit 3D sensor inputs such as depth maps or point clouds, but these approaches face challenges due to sensor noise, hardware heterogeneity, and incomplete depth coverage in existing datasets. Alternative methods that estimate 3D cues from 2D images also suffer from the limited performance of depth estimators. We propose Spatial Forcing (SF), a simple yet effective alignment strategy that implicitly forces VLA models to develop spatial comprehension capabilities without relying on explicit 3D inputs or depth estimators. SF aligns intermediate visual embeddings of VLAs with geometric representations produced by pretrained 3D foundation models. By enforcing alignment at intermediate layers, SF guides VLAs to encode richer spatial representations that enhance action precision. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that SF achieves state-of-the-art results, surpassing both 2D- and 3D-based VLAs. SF further accelerates training by up to 3.8× and improves data efficiency across diverse robotic tasks. Project page: https://spatial-forcing.github.io/.

sections.body:
The introduction argues that VLAs built on 2D-pretrained vision-language models lack precise spatial awareness. Explicit depth or point-cloud inputs suffer from sensor noise, hardware heterogeneity and incomplete depth coverage, and depth-estimator methods are limited by estimator quality.

To test the gap, the authors freeze the visual embeddings of a mainstream VLA and train only a DPT head to predict depth maps. Fig. 1(c) shows that the original embeddings do not yield meaningful spatial structures.

The proposed Spatial Forcing (SF) aligns intermediate visual embeddings with representations from VGGT, a pretrained 3D foundation model. The authors report top results on LIBERO and RoboTwin, training up to 3.8× faster, and better data efficiency.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Depth probing shows that a mainstream VLA's visual embeddings lack meaningful spatial structure.

sections.body:
The method aligns the visual tokens of a VLA with spatial features from VGGT. Multi-view images pass through VGGT, and each VLA visual token passes through batch normalization and a two-layer MLP. A cosine-similarity loss then pulls each token toward the spatial feature at its pixel location, with positional embedding added to the target.

The total training objective is:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SF}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}
$$

where alpha weights the alignment term. The authors find that supervising relatively deep layers, but not the deepest ones, is most effective. At inference the trained model matches a standard VLA and adds no structures or computational overhead. The evidence is the depth probing in Fig. 3 and the component experiments that follow.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Spatial Forcing adds an alignment loss on intermediate visual tokens and adds no inference cost.

sections.body:
Simulation tests use LIBERO, with four task suites, and RoboTwin. On LIBERO, SF is built on OpenVLA-OFT and gets the best performance across all four suites among methods without extra sensor inputs. The authors state that SF reaches performance comparable to GeoVLA and 3D-CAVLA, which use extra depth or point-cloud inputs.

On RoboTwin, SF is built on π0 and has the highest average success rate, with improvements over π0 across all tasks. The authors credit the larger gains on hard, domain-randomized tasks to better capture of object locations.

Ablations use OpenVLA-OFT on a single H100. VGGT as the target gives the highest success rates, and aligning the 24th layer works best. With 5% of the data, SF reaches 75.8% success, and training with alignment reaches the same success 3.8× faster. The authors state that ablations were limited by computational resources.
sections.heading: Simulation Experiments
sections.headline: Spatial Forcing gets the best results among methods without extra sensors and the highest RoboTwin average, reaching equal success 3.8× faster.

sections.body:
Real-world tests run on a bimanual AgileX platform with two 6-DoF Piper arms, one primary camera and two wrist cameras. Single-arm tasks are trained on 40 demonstrations and the bimanual task on 20. Single-arm tasks use 10 trials per variation, 40 in total, and the bimanual task uses 20 trials.

The text reports higher success rates on all tasks. For stacking glass cups, SF reaches 47.5% higher success than the base model. For placing a green block at varied heights, SF reaches an 85% success rate.

The grasp vegetable and lift pot tasks are described qualitatively, without numbers. The authors present the results as evidence of data efficiency, but the tests cover only these four tasks and these sample sizes.
sections.heading: Real-world Experiments
sections.headline: Spatial Forcing improves real-robot success on all four tasks, reaching 85% on the green block task.

sections.body:
Earlier VLA work improves spatial perception by estimating depth, injecting point clouds, or projecting spatial information. The authors note that these methods enrich only the visual inputs and overlook that intermediate visual embeddings also shape the action tokens.

Representation supervision appears in two forms. Reconstruction methods, including ReconVLA and ROSS, reconstruct images from features. The authors argue that reconstruction may not suit VLAs because it fails to filter out redundant details.

Alignment methods, including REPA and 3DRS, match intermediate hidden states to external encoders. The authors follow this alignment approach and target geometry-aware structures.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior VLAs add spatial information to inputs, while alignment-based supervision has been used in image and video generation.

sections.body:
The conclusion restates the depth probing finding that the original VLA embeddings lack spatial structure. It then restates the alignment method, which uses external spatial representations from 3D foundation models.

It states that simulation experiments show improved performance, faster training, and better data efficiency. It states that real-world experiments show spatial comprehension across diverse robotic tasks.

The conclusion adds no new numbers and does not discuss limitations beyond the reported experiments.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Spatial Forcing aligns VLA visual embeddings with 3D foundation features, improving performance, training speed, and data efficiency.

sections.body:
Appendix A sweeps the alignment weight alpha over 0, 0.02, 0.1, 0.5, 2.5 and 12.5. Success is 73.2% at 0, reaches 93.6% at 0.5, and falls to 81.2% at 12.5. The authors state that an excessively large weight may destabilize the visual modality, and 0.5 is the default.

Appendix B explains the t-SNE plots. It argues that matching cluster shape without overlapping cluster centers shows that alignment does not collapse the VLA features into the target.

Appendix C describes teleoperated data collection at 30Hz, recording camera images and joint angles, with separate fine-tuning per task. Appendix D summarizes the compared models, including π0, OpenVLA-OFT and Diffusion Policy.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers the alignment-weight sweep, t-SNE interpretation, real-world data collection, and compared-model descriptions.
